summary: Describes state machines for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) peer and for several kinds of authenticators: stand-alone, backend, and full. The state machines show how EAP can be implemented in different deployments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4137 describes how EAP peers and authenticators can manage an authentication exchange. It shows the states, signals, and transitions for local and backend authentication arrangements, while allowing implementations to use other designs.

questions: what is an eap state machine
subtitle: State-machine descriptions for EAP peers, authenticators, and backend servers.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) supports different authentication methods, and implementers need a clear account of how peers and authenticators manage the exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes state machines for a peer, a stand-alone authenticator, a backend authenticator, and a full authenticator that can use local or pass-through methods.
tldr.outcome: The state machines are illustrative, not mandatory implementation designs. RFCs 3748 and 3579 remain authoritative where they differ from this document.

today: RFC 4137 is an Informational RFC published in August 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC says RFCs 3748 and 3579 remain authoritative where they differ.

sections.title: The EAP Switch Model
sections.content:
Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) authentication uses one or more methods, followed by an EAP Success or EAP Failure message from the authenticator. An EAP Switch coordinates the method or sequence of methods at the peer and authenticator.

This RFC describes state machines for the peer, a stand-alone authenticator, a backend authenticator, and a full authenticator that supports local and pass-through methods. The model is informative: implementations may achieve the same results in other ways.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP uses a shared exchange format for different authentication methods. The state machines show how each side can choose a method, exchange messages, and finish the conversation.

sections.title: How to Read a State Machine
sections.content:
A state machine has a set of mutually exclusive states, with only one state active at a time. Arrows show allowed transitions, and labels give the conditions for taking each transition.

When a machine enters a state, it runs that state's listed procedures in order. The machine then evaluates transition conditions until one is met. The RFC says that, if its state diagram conflicts with its transition table or description, the diagram takes precedence; RFC 3748 or RFC 3579 takes precedence over this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A state machine describes one active state and the conditions for moving to another. The actions listed for a state run when the machine enters it.

sections.title: Peer State Machine
sections.content:
The peer machine waits for a packet from the lower layer, parses it, and directs requests to an identity handler, notification handler, or EAP method. The method processes the request and may produce a response, which the peer passes back to the lower layer for transmission.

The peer machine tracks the method's state and the result it expects. EAP Success and EAP Failure lead to final success and failure states. The peer state machine described in the RFC has 13 states.
sections.plainLanguage: The peer receives a request, sends it to the right handler or method, and returns any response through the lower layer. The exchange ends when the peer accepts an EAP Success or EAP Failure message.

sections.title: Stand-Alone, Backend, and Full Authenticators
sections.content:
A stand-alone authenticator selects methods, sends requests, processes responses, and decides whether to succeed or fail. It can retransmit a request and can enter a timeout-failure state when it receives no response.

A backend authenticator runs on an AAA server and can continue a method started by a pass-through authenticator. A full authenticator combines local methods with pass-through to a backend. The RFC gives separate state machines for these arrangements.
sections.plainLanguage: A stand-alone authenticator handles methods itself. A backend arrangement sends the exchange to an AAA server, while a full authenticator can use either approach.

sections.title: Implementation and Interoperability
sections.content:
Some state procedures may take a long time, such as waiting for a user to provide an identity or waiting for a method to process a message. Implementations may use separate threads or add timeouts so a delayed procedure does not block the state machine indefinitely.

The RFC describes a possible workaround for deployed authenticators that increment the EAP identifier incorrectly in Success or Failure messages. It says the workaround is not recommended because it does not conform to RFC 3748 and should be optional if implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations need to account for slow user input and methods that do not return promptly. The RFC also documents a non-standard workaround for some existing authenticators.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says an accurate state machine can reduce implementation errors, while RFC 3748 remains the normative protocol description. Identity, NAK, Success, and Failure packets are not cryptographically protected by themselves, so an attacker may insert or modify them.

The document describes denial-of-service cases involving a forged Failure, repeated Identity requests, or a NAK sent after a method is proposed. It warns that changing initial variable values to prevent these cases can also break legitimate exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: Some EAP messages are not protected by cryptography on their own and can be forged or changed. Clear state-machine rules can help avoid implementation errors, but workarounds must not break valid exchanges.
